Identify the dominant error signature (deadline-exceeded vs connection errors vs timeouts vs 5xx) and whether pricing-engine's own resource metrics (CPU, memory, GC, thread/connection pool, outbound call latency) are saturated. Report per-minute timeline from 12:30 to 14:59.

Enumerate EVERY change across all services in the window 2026-04-08T00:00Z to 2026-04-09T14:59Z (deployments and config/feature-flag changes), regardless of the reporter's claim that no pricing releases happened. Specifically look for changes in pricing-engine or anything it depends on, any change landing shortly before/at the onset window ~13:00-13:30, and whether any change was reverted. Also report pricing-engine's direct and transitive dependencies, and flag any shared component used by multiple latency-affected services. Additionally search historical incidents for prior 'quote latency / deadline exceeded pricing-engine' occurrences and their root cause.

events.statement: Exactly one deployment occurred across all services in the full incident window: dep-5604, auth-service v7.2.0 ('Session cookie hardening', change SameSite=strict), deployed 2026-04-09T11:30:00Z by ci-bot, status 'live' with rolled_back_at=null (no revert).
The Apr 8 portion of the window (2026-04-08T00:00Z–2026-04-09T00:00Z) contains zero deployments, completing the enumeration: no deployment touched pricing-engine or any dependency on Apr 8.
No config or feature-flag changes were recorded for any service in the window (both the full 04-08→04-09 window and the narrowed 2026-04-09T11:00Z→14:59Z window returned count 0).

pricing-engine's dependency graph: direct callees market-data-service (http) and redis-cache (cache); market-data-service further calls redis-cache (cache) and exchange-gateway (http); order-service calls pricing-engine (http) and api-gateway calls order-service. No pricing-engine edge appears in the change set.

redis-cache is the SHARED component in pricing-engine's dependency graph (shared=true, owner platform) and is used by BOTH pricing-engine and market-data-service, making a shared cache a plausible cross-service propagation path for latency.

The single change in the window (auth-service v7.2.0 at 11:30Z) is absent from pricing-engine's dependency graph and landed ~1.5h before the ~13:00–13:30 onset; the closest historical analogue to the reported symptom 'quote latency / cache' is HIST-107 'Cold cache storm after redis failover' (redis-cache + market-data-service, category infrastructure_failure), and HIST-113 is a pricing-engine capacity/cpu saturation 'quote timeouts' precedent.

events.statement: pricing-engine p99 latency was steady at ~56-64ms through 13:21:00Z, then jumped to 2227.82ms at 13:22:00Z — a step change, not gradual. Onset is 13:22:00Z (first minute bucket above 1s), rising slightly to a peak of 2309.91ms at 13:26Z, then slowly declining to ~1141ms by 14:58Z (still well above baseline).

pricing-engine error_rate (HTTP 5xx %) was ~0.15-0.28% before onset, then stepped to 3.21% at 13:22Z and held a plateau of ~3.9-4.3% through 14:58Z. So both latency and 5xx errors have the same 13:22Z onset and step-change shape.

The dominant error signature is deadline-exceeded, not connection errors: 192/194 matched pricing-engine log entries are ERROR with pattern 'quote computation deadline exceeded: market-data-service took <n>ms', first seen 13:23:57Z ('took 5171ms'), last 14:58:47Z. Individual outbound call times range from 827ms to 8456ms.

pricing-engine's own resource metrics are NOT saturated: cpu_pct stayed flat at ~34.6-44.5% across the entire window (39.8% avg at 13:30Z, 40.63% at 14:40Z), and memory_pct stayed flat at ~43.4-54.9% (49.51% at 13:30Z, 48.48% at 14:50Z). Neither metric moved at the 13:22Z onset — the latency rise is not from CPU/memory pressure on pricing-engine.

market-data-service shows a 'cache miss storm' starting at exactly 13:22:25Z: 289 WARN entries 'cache miss storm: quote:<id> not in redis-cache, rebuilding from exchange feed snapshot (<n>ms)' from 13:22:25Z to 14:58:22Z, with rebuild times of 1034-8748ms. This starts at the same minute as pricing-engine's latency jump and matches the deadline-exceeded errors naming market-data-service.

Blast radius beyond pricing-engine is not yet confirmed from metrics: the api-gateway and redis-cache latency queries (and pricing-engine request_rate) could not be executed because the tool-call budget was exhausted. Only pricing-engine (latency + error rate step at 13:22Z) and market-data-service (cache-miss storm from 13:22:25Z) have direct metric/log evidence of impact.

events.summary: The 13:22Z onset and the pricing-engine symptom chain (p99 step, 5xx step, deadline-exceeded errors naming market-data-service, market-data-service 'cache miss storm') are well verified (F7-F11). What is NOT established is the ORIGIN of the cache-miss storm: H1 blames a shared redis-cache failure/eviction storm, H2 blames market-data-service's own rebuild/feed path, H4 blames load. No redis-cache metric, no market-data-service latency/health metric, and no request_rate was ever retrieved, so the ranking between H1 (0.40) and H2 (0.30) rests entirely on a structural assumption ('redis-cache degraded') that the reasoning agent itself lists as an assumption. H2 currently even has the stronger direct evidence (market-data-service rebuild times 1034-8748ms = slow rebuilds) but is listed as contradicting F5, which is a topology fact, not a contradiction. H3 is properly rejected (no graph edge, 1h52m silent gap, no auth signature). H4 is unverified but low-impact (its fix overlaps H1/H2 sizing). The decisive, obtainable evidence is redis-cache health metrics at 13:22Z and whether market-data-service itself restarted/latency-stepped — one observability round should separate H1 from H2. The H1 causal chain's final hop ('slow quotes in trading screens, blast radius unconfirmed') is inferred, not verified.

events.statement: redis-cache hit_ratio_pct collapsed from a steady ~95-96% baseline to 11.55% in the 13:22:00Z bucket, then slowly recovered (14.88% 13:30, 47.74% 14:58) — a step change at exactly the minute pricing-engine and market-data-service stepped, not a gradual decline.

redis-cache memory_pct collapsed in the same 13:22:00Z bucket from ~68-71% (13:18 avg 70.54) to 6.38% (max 6.81), i.e. the cache contents were dropped/reset at ~13:22Z rather than merely under memory pressure. It then climbs steadily (6.38%→29.94% by 14:58), the signature of a cache being re-populated from cold.

redis-cache evictions_per_min did NOT spike at 13:22Z: it stayed flat at ~2.3-3.7 keys/min across the whole window (13:18 avg 3.29, 13:22 avg 3.11, 14:58 avg 2.32; overall max 4.87). So the cache emptying was NOT an eviction/memory-pressure storm — consistent with an external reset/restart/flush or failover rather than maxmemory-driven eviction.

market-data-service's OWN latency p99 stepped at the same 13:22:00Z bucket: avg 39.8ms/40.92ms through 13:18, then 1916.65ms at 13:22, peak max 1979.98ms, decaying to 874.6ms by 14:58 — the identical step-and-decay shape as redis-cache's hit-ratio/memory reset, and its error_rate also stepped 0.18%→3.23% at 13:22Z.

Temporal ordering within the onset minute favors the cache: redis-cache's hit-ratio/memory reset occupies the 13:22:00Z bucket, pricing-engine's p99 step is at 13:22:00Z, and market-data-service's 'cache miss storm' WARN log (F11, from team) first appears at 13:22:25Z — the cache metric reset is not later than the rebuild storm that names it.

events.answer: redis-cache itself stepped at exactly the 13:22Z minute: hit_ratio collapsed 95.33%→11.55% and memory_pct collapsed 70.54%→6.38% in the same 13:22 bucket, i.e. the cache was emptied/reset at ~13:22Z (evictions and CPU stayed flat, so not a memory-pressure eviction storm). This cache-side reset precedes/coincides with the market-data-service step (its own p99 stepped 39.8ms→1916.65ms at 13:22Z) and with the pricing-engine step (13:22Z), consistent with H1's origin hop being the shared redis-cache rather than a fault isolated inside market-data-service. I could NOT verify market-data-service's own cpu/memory/restarts/request_rate (budget exhausted), so a concurrent service-side restart/saturation at 13:22Z cannot be excluded; the exchange-gateway-vs-cache wait-time correlation is also unresolved.

Load-driven capacity saturation / cold-cache storm from traffic, with no triggering change

events.summary: Round 2 delivered the decisive evidence my round-1 review demanded. The origin hop was the open question, and it is now resolved in H1's favor by direct measurement rather than assumption: redis-cache's own hit_ratio_pct collapsed 95.33%→11.55% and memory_pct collapsed 70.54%→6.38% in the *same* 13:22Z bucket (F19, F20) while evictions_per_min stayed flat at ~2.3-3.7/min (F21) — a genuine cache-content reset, not memory-pressure eviction. That reset is not later than the market-data-service rebuild storm it names (13:22Z vs 13:22:25Z, F23), and market-data-service's own p99/error_rate step in that same bucket (F22). The failure shape is a single-minute step with slow cold re-warm, at *constant* load (request_rate flat ~641.9 req/s, 647.09 in the onset bucket, F13), which kills H4's mechanism outright. The observed service is a symptom, not the cause: pricing-engine's CPU/memory are flat (F10) and its dominant error is 'deadline exceeded: market-data-service took 827-8456ms' (F9), i.e. it is blocked on the cold cache path. H3 was independently killed on four fronts (no graph edge F4, 1h52m silent gap + no revert F6, wrong error signature F9, zero 401/403/auth log matches F14/F15) plus flat upstream error rates (F16/F17). H2 remains a live alternative only in the narrow sense that a *concurrent* market-data-service-side restart/saturation was never excluded because its cpu/memory/restarts metrics returned budget_exhausted; but H2's own origin hop is still labeled ASSUMED and requires denying the cache's independent memory/hit collapse, which F20 makes hard. Per the review rubric, that is a residual secondary uncertainty to be capped, not a reason to hold the incident open. The chain's remaining unverified hop (user-facing blast radius at api-gateway/order-service) is a scope detail of a proven origin, not an origin question, and does not change which fix applies. I therefore accept at a capped confidence that reflects the unexcluded concurrent-market-data-service-restart alternative and the unmeasured upstream latency.

critiques.summary: Round 2 delivered the decisive evidence my round-1 review demanded. The origin hop was the open question, and it is now resolved in H1's favor by direct measurement rather than assumption: redis-cache's own hit_ratio_pct collapsed 95.33%→11.55% and memory_pct collapsed 70.54%→6.38% in the *same* 13:22Z bucket (F19, F20) while evictions_per_min stayed flat at ~2.3-3.7/min (F21) — a genuine cache-content reset, not memory-pressure eviction. That reset is not later than the market-data-service rebuild storm it names (13:22Z vs 13:22:25Z, F23), and market-data-service's own p99/error_rate step in that same bucket (F22). The failure shape is a single-minute step with slow cold re-warm, at *constant* load (request_rate flat ~641.9 req/s, 647.09 in the onset bucket, F13), which kills H4's mechanism outright. The observed service is a symptom, not the cause: pricing-engine's CPU/memory are flat (F10) and its dominant error is 'deadline exceeded: market-data-service took 827-8456ms' (F9), i.e. it is blocked on the cold cache path. H3 was independently killed on four fronts (no graph edge F4, 1h52m silent gap + no revert F6, wrong error signature F9, zero 401/403/auth log matches F14/F15) plus flat upstream error rates (F16/F17). H2 remains a live alternative only in the narrow sense that a *concurrent* market-data-service-side restart/saturation was never excluded because its cpu/memory/restarts metrics returned budget_exhausted; but H2's own origin hop is still labeled ASSUMED and requires denying the cache's independent memory/hit collapse, which F20 makes hard. Per the review rubric, that is a residual secondary uncertainty to be capped, not a reason to hold the incident open. The chain's remaining unverified hop (user-facing blast radius at api-gateway/order-service) is a scope detail of a proven origin, not an origin question, and does not change which fix applies. I therefore accept at a capped confidence that reflects the unexcluded concurrent-market-data-service-restart alternative and the unmeasured upstream latency.

challenges.issue: The mechanism hop (external flush/restart/failover of redis-cache) is still inferred, not observed: redis-cache exposes no restart/uptime/latency metric, so 'external reset' rests on the joint hit_ratio+memory collapse plus flat evictions. The inference is sound and the evictions-flat observation (F21) does constrain the alternatives, but the specific trigger (flush vs failover vs rolling restart) is undetermined and no enumerable change exists (F1, F3).

Final hop is unverified: user-facing blast radius (api-gateway/order-service latency) was never measured, and api-gateway/order-service error rates are flat (F16, F17). The reported '2-3s quotes' is therefore grounded only in pricing-engine p99 (2227.82ms) and the deadline-exceeded errors, not measured at the API layer.

Not conclusively refuted: market-data-service's own cpu_pct/memory_pct/restarts/request_rate were never retrieved (budget_exhausted), so a concurrent market-data-service-side restart or saturation at 13:22Z remains formally possible. This is the single largest residual uncertainty and is what holds the confidence cap below 0.8. It is weakened (not closed) by F20: a service-side stall cannot by itself collapse the cache's absolute memory_pct to 6.38%.

Its origin hop — 'market-data-service's snapshot rebuild path slows at 13:22Z (exchange-gateway latency or internal saturation)' — has zero supporting evidence (self-labeled ASSUMED) and no deployment touched market-data-service or exchange-gateway in the window (F1). It is a mechanism asserted to fit the observed rebuild times, not a finding.

Mechanism is contradicted, not merely unsupported: request_rate was flat at the onset (F13) and pricing-engine CPU/memory flat (F10), so the load-surge mechanism has no evidence and the step-at-constant-load shape rules out gradual capacity exhaustion. Correctly ranked last; retained only as a sizing consideration.

Rejection is well grounded (F4, F6, F9, F14, F15, F16, F17). One residual: api-gateway 401/403 absence is confirmed only at WARN level (the INFO-level search timed out, tc-029), so 'zero auth signature at all log levels' is not fully proven. This does not revive H3 given the graph-edge and timing failures.
